newsitem.title: USA: Western power market shrugs off Intertie cuts.
newsitem.headline: Western power market shrugs off Intertie cuts.

text.p: Capacity restrictions on the Pacific Intertie are unlikely to have a big impact on the power market this spring due to the abundance of hydropower resources throughout the West, industry sources said.
"Prices are already going to be depressed because California will need to use its (water) instead of spilling it," said one utility wholesale marketer.
Typically in the spring, net flows on the intertie lines will shift from northbound to southbound, as the Southwest begins to use more power than the Northwest.
Power from the Pacific Northwest is also usually cost competitive for such long-distance transmissions due to the region's abundance of spring hydropower generation.
This year, however, the AC and DC intertie lines will run at no more than 6,250 megawatts (MW), compared with a rated capacity of 7,900 MW due to voltage support worries.
Since two major power outages swept the West last summer, the lines have been capped at 5,200 MW, but the rate is expected to be lifted by about 25 percent late next month.
A technical group has approved the rate increase, but final approval from the Western Systems Coordinating Council is not expected before mid- to late March.
Nevertheless, market sources say the lack of capacity into the Southwest will not be a big factor for power prices, since supplies throughout the region are likely to be abundant.
National Weather Service forecasts call for spring runoff in both the Northwest and California at around 140 percent of average rates seen in the past 30 years.
"Prices will stay depressed," said one utility trader.
The Southwest will see higher demand in the spring and summer, but California's high hydropower output will alleviate any shortfall in transmissions from the Northwest, he noted.
"Potentially, Northwest (hydropower) producers could sell more (without intertie restrictions), but there will be a lot of competition between sellers anyway," said another trader.
